item.title: Quantum Simulation of Markovian and Non-Markovian Open Quantum Dynamics in Heavy-Ion Collisions
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Non-Markovian open quantum dynamics for heavy-ion probes can be simulated via an auxiliary two-level pseudomode qubit coupled to a memoryless bath, which requires one extra persistent qubit and smoothly converges to the Markovian limit as τc→0.

Grade 0.370 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum machine learning” · Doojin Kim, Balbeer Singh

Figure

Bound-state survival probability Pbound(t) plotted versus time t for non-Markovian quantum-circuit simulations at memory times τc=10.0,5.0,0.5 GeV−1 compared to the Markovian solution at τc=0.1 GeV−1.

Asks

How can open-quantum-system dynamics beyond the Markovian limit be simulated efficiently on a quantum computer for hard probes in heavy-ion collisions?

But

Two-level bound-state subsystem, static and homogeneous thermal medium, exponentially decaying medium correlation function, weak subsystem-bath coupling.

Tools

pseudomode method · Kraus map / Stinespring dilation · symmetric operator splitting · pNRQED dipole coupling

Abstract

We present a quantum computing framework for simulating open-quantum-system approaches based on Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics, which is relevant to heavy-ion collisions. To simulate the non-Markovian evolution on quantum computers, we introduce an auxiliary two-level pseudomode that carries the memory forward and couples to both the subsystem and the residual Markovian bath. We explicitly show that tracing out the pseudomode reproduces the non-Markovian evolution with the exact memory kernel. Moreover, in the relevant time scale hierarchy, the quantum circuit construction of the pseudomode smoothly converges to the Markovian limit. For a given bath memory kernel, our results demonstrate the feasibility of quantum simulations of both Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics, establishing a framework for future studies of hard probes such as jets, heavy quarks, and quarkonia in heavy-ion collisions.

item.title: "Train classical, deploy quantum" requires rethinking generalization
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Deploy-quantum models trained by classically matching low-order moments or MMD2 fail to generalize: IQP Born machine coverage decouples from loss and remains near the random baseline Crand, while matching low-order correlators allows exact minimizers with support coverage as small as 0.07.

Grade 0.365 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Effect of data encoding on the expressive power of variational quantum-machine-…” · Snehal Raj, Natansh Mathur, Alejandro Perdomo-Ortiz

Figure

Training loss (gray) and sample coverage (red) plotted across optimization steps and model sizes for IQP Born machines and likelihood-trained classical models. IQP training reduces loss by an order of magnitude while coverage remains flat near the random baseline floor.

Asks

Does minimizing classical moment-matching loss functions lead to quantum generative models that generalize rather than merely memorize training statistics?

But

State-vector simulation up to N=30 qubits; tested only on cardinality-constrained and genomic single-nucleotide variant datasets where validity is known.

Tools

IQP Born machines · Fermionic Born machines (FBM) · Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD²) · Tensor-network Born machines (TNBM) · Direct sample coverage and forward KL divergence benchmarking

Abstract

Generative models have become central across science and industry, from image and text synthesis to the design of molecules and materials. Quantum generative models are considered one of the most promising applications for quantum computers, since a quantum circuit naturally produces samples from the distribution it encodes, and for suitable circuits that distribution is believed to be hard for any classical computer to reproduce. A leading strategy trains these models on a classical computer and reserves the quantum device for generating samples at deployment. This is possible when the training loss can be evaluated on a classical computer. A prime example is the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD²), a moment-matching loss that compares the model and the data through their Pauli-Z correlations. Research so far has asked whether such models can be trained and whether their sampling is hard; whether minimizing such an objective yields a model that generalizes, rather than one that merely reproduces the training statistics, remains poorly understood. We benchmark a broad set of quantum and classical generative models by direct sampling and show that models trained with a moment-matching loss generally show worse generalization than the likelihood-trained models. We show this on two application-inspired datasets: first a cardinality-constrained dataset at up to 30 qubits and second a dataset of genomic single-nucleotide variants, whose valid set is the observed data. These results indicate that a converged moment-matching loss is not a reliable measure of generalization, and that train-classical, deploy-quantum workflows will need approaches that target generalization directly, leaving open whether better training objectives suffice or whether the model architectures themselves must change.

item.title: Representation Learning with Quantum Signal Processing
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Calculates exact mean and variance of the quantum neural tangent kernel for degree-d quantum signal processing. Normalized diagonal 3Kd(x,x)/M converges in distribution to Beta⁡(3/2,1/2) with asymptotic coefficient of variation 1/3, remaining non-self-averaging despite SU(2) Haar mixing.

Grade 0.354 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Machine Learning in Feature Hilbert Spaces” · Junqi Wang, Junyu Liu

Figure

Diagonal normalized kernel distribution matching the Beta⁡(3/2,1/2) law (left), coefficient of variation approaching 1/3 versus depth (middle), and the angular profile of the mean kernel approaching a Gaussian with width O(d−1/2) (right).

Asks

Does a provable training law hold for quantum models when the realized quantum neural tangent kernel is random at initialization and evolves during learning?

But

Sparse data regime requiring n3/2(1+log⁡n)/M→0 with rescaled time τ=Mt/(3n) over finite interval T; single-qubit model.

Tools

quantum signal processing · quantum neural tangent kernel · replicated transfer processes · continuous gradient flow · Grönwall estimate

Abstract

Representation learning begins when training changes the features that define similarity between data. A frozen-kernel model only reweights a fixed geometry. We establish quantum signal processing (QSP) as a solvable quantum model of the representation-learning regime. At arbitrary depth, we compute the exact mean and variance of its quantum neural tangent kernel, revealing an input-dependent angular geometry whose diagonal remains non-self-averaging even when the underlying unitary approaches Haar randomness. We also prove a sparse-data guarantee for the full nonlinear gradient flow without freezing or ensemble-averaging the kernel: the realized dynamics converges to an integrable scalar flow with a time-dependent kernel closure and explicit convergence times. A finite-depth speed limit holds for every data set and trajectory. At higher data density, numerical results show coupled evolution beyond both the scalar and frozen-kernel descriptions. These results give a controlled theory of learned quantum data geometry with provable training dynamics beyond the frozen limit.

item.title: Quantum Pessiland
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Constructed oracle separations showing Quantum Pessiland: 𝖴𝖯∩𝖼𝗈𝖴𝖯 is strongly hard on average against quantum polynomial-time algorithms with quantum advice, yet auxiliary-input EFI pairs (relative to a quantum oracle) and classically-secure auxiliary-input one-way puzzles (relative to a classical oracle where 𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝖡𝖰𝖯=𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝖡𝖯𝖯) do not exist.

Grade 0.342 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum machine learning models built from interference and oracle algorithms,…” · Boyang Chen, Tomoyuki Morimae, Takashi Yamakawa

Asks

Is there a quantum analogue of Pessiland where 𝖭𝖯 is hard on average but quantum cryptography does not exist?

Before

Wee (2005) constructed classical Pessiland where 𝖴𝖯∩𝖼𝗈𝖴𝖯 is average-case hard but classical one-way functions do not exist; whether quantum cryptography could survive on average-case hard 𝖭𝖯 remained open.

But

Results hold in relativized oracle models (classical and quantum oracle worlds).

Tools

Random permutation verification oracles · Quantified Boolean formula (QBF) oracle · Hierarchical quantum state measurement oracle · Oracle patching lemma · Goldreich-Levin theorem with quantum advice

Abstract

Pessiland is a world where NP is hard on average but one-way functions (OWFs) do not exist [Impagliazzo 1995]. Because almost all classical cryptographic primitives imply OWFs [Impagliazzo and Luby 1989], there is almost no classical cryptography in Pessiland. On the other hand, quantum cryptography can exist even when OWFs do not [Kretschmer 2021; Morimae and Yamakawa 2022; Ananth, Qian and Yuen 2022]. Is there a quantum analogue of Pessiland where NP is hard on average but even quantum cryptography does not exist? In this paper, we show that such a miserable world, Quantum Pessiland, exists: there is a quantum oracle relative to which UP∩coUP is hard on average against quantum polynomial-time algorithms with quantum advice, yet auxiliary-input EFI pairs do not exist. We also show that there is a classical oracle relative to which UP∩coUP is hard on average against quantum polynomial-time algorithms with quantum advice, yet classically-secure auxiliary-input one-way puzzles (OWPuzzs) do not exist. Almost all quantum cryptographic primitives imply EFI pairs or OWPuzzs, and therefore these results mean that there is almost no quantum cryptography relative to these oracles. We further show that relative to the classical oracle, SampBQP = SampBPP, and therefore there is no sampling-based quantum advantage in Quantum Pessiland. Finally, because our average-case hardness of UP∩coUP implies P^(#P)not⊆i.o.BQP/qpoly, our result also implies that a non-relativizing proof technique is necessary to construct OWPuzzs solely from P^(#P)not⊆i.o.BQP/qpoly, which gives a partial negative answer to the open problem of [Khurana and Tomer 2025].

item.title: Data and code for collision-model Dicke-state preparation: depth-fidelity frontiers, circuit costs, and superconducting-processor measurements
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Presents dataset across 31 Dicke target states DNK (N=5 to 14, depth m=0 to 200 sub-rounds) and hardware benchmarks on the 54-qubit IQM Emerald processor, where measured circuits retain up to 0.758 of noiseless fidelity.

Grade 0.341 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Power of data in quantum machine learning” · Duc-Kha Vu, Minh Tam Nguyen, cSahin K. Özdemir, Özgür E. Müstecapliouglu, Fatih Ozaydin

Figure

Unconditional state fidelity F across hardware measurement arms on the IQM Emerald superconducting processor compared to the ideal noiseless fidelity Fideal and native two-qubit gate count.

Asks

How do state-preparation fidelity, circuit depth, and hardware gate overhead trade off when generating multipartite Dicke states via collision models?

But

Circuit depth capped at m=200 sub-rounds; noiseless L1 yields lower bounds rather than certified global optima; 544 of 6,231 cost rows are upper bounds; hardware results reflect a single session on 10 arms without physical excitation-number heralding.

Tools

collision model quantum state preparation · IQM Emerald 54-qubit superconducting processor · permutation-orbit tomography · Qiskit

Abstract

Dicke states are multipartite entangled states in which a fixed number of quantum excitations is coherently shared among many qubits. Originally introduced in the context of cooperative emission and superradiance, they are now important resources for quantum sensing, networking, and collective quantum phenomena. Preparing prescribed Dicke states with high fidelity, however, remains challenging, particularly as the system size and excitation number increase. Here we present an open dataset and accompanying code for preparing Dicke states using a collision-based quantum protocol. The dataset covers systems from five to fourteen qubits over a broad range of excitation numbers and records how the best-found noiseless preparation fidelity changes with circuit depth. It also provides circuit-resource estimates and experimental measurements for selected states on the 54-qubit IQM Emerald superconducting processor. The accompanying code reproduces the processed data and validation checks, providing a reusable benchmark for studying the trade-off between state-preparation fidelity, circuit cost, and hardware noise.

item.title: Hardware-Efficient Exchange-Only QML: Singlet-Triplet Spin Chains via Inter-pair Coupling without Magnetic Gradients
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Linear chain of 6 semiconductor spins with isotropic Heisenberg exchange alone (no ΔBz) achieves 90.99%±0.24% test accuracy on full 10,000-image MNIST, reaching 88.1% with linear readout.

Grade 0.334 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Power of data in quantum machine learning” · Yuichiro Minato

Figure

Confusion matrix across all 10 digit classes for the 6-spin TE-EX model on the full 10,000-image MNIST test set, showing an overall accuracy of 90.89%.

Asks

Can quantum machine learning achieve high expressibility on two-spin units using only isotropic Heisenberg exchange interactions without magnetic field gradients or multi-spin logical encodings?

Before

Classical linear baseline on identical 12 PCA components achieves 83.2%, and frozen random exchange dynamics (reservoir) reaches 53.0%.

But

Numerical simulation of 6 spins in the Mz=0 subspace; tested against quasi-static pulse-area noise up to 10% and finite shot noise (103 shots) but without finite-bandwidth charge noise or hyperfine dephasing.

Tools

Time-Encoded Exchange (TE-EX) protocol · Heisenberg exchange Hamiltonian · Néel state initialization · Principal Component Analysis (PCA) · Batch Normalization

Code. https://github.com/minatoyuichiro/teex-mnist

Abstract

Standard universal quantum computing using exchange-only qubits typically requires three physical spins per logical qubit, leading to significant hardware overhead. Conversely, two-spin units offer higher density but rely on local magnetic field gradients for control, increasing integration complexity. In this paper, we propose a resource-efficient quantum machine learning (QML) architecture that achieves high expressibility using minimal two-spin units and Heisenberg exchange interactions alone, without any magnetic gradients. We shift the paradigm from universal gate-based control to utilizing the intrinsic, time-domain dynamics of a spin chain as a learning resource. Numerical simulations on MNIST digit classification demonstrate that the symmetry-protected constraints of isolated spin pairs are bypassed by leveraging inter-pair exchange coupling. This interference-mediated state mixing significantly enhances the expressibility of the Hilbert space. The model reaches a test-set accuracy of 90.9% +/- 0.2% over five independent seeds on the full 10,000-image MNIST test set. Under an identical linear readout, the trained quantum feature map (88.1%) clearly outperforms a classical linear baseline on the same PCA inputs (83.2%) as well as an untrained (reservoir-style) version of the same dynamics (53.0%), demonstrating that the learned, input-dependent exchange pulses implement a genuinely non-linear and trainable feature map. The protocol is also robust to experimentally relevant imperfections: accuracy remains at 89.9% under 10% quasi-static pulse-area noise and at 89.8% when every observable is estimated from 10^3 measurement shots. These findings suggest that competitive QML can be executed on the simplest possible semiconductor spin-chain hardware, bypassing the need for leakage-prone encodings or complex micro-magnet integration.

item.arxave:abstract: Standard universal quantum computing using exchange-only qubits typically requires three physical spins per logical qubit, leading to significant hardware overhead. Conversely, two-spin units offer higher density but rely on local magnetic field gradients for control, increasing integration complexity. In this paper, we propose a resource-efficient quantum machine learning (QML) architecture that achieves high expressibility using minimal two-spin units and Heisenberg exchange interactions alone, without any magnetic gradients. We shift the paradigm from universal gate-based control to utilizing the intrinsic, time-domain dynamics of a spin chain as a learning resource. Numerical simulations on MNIST digit classification demonstrate that the symmetry-protected constraints of isolated spin pairs are bypassed by leveraging inter-pair exchange coupling. This interference-mediated state mixing significantly enhances the expressibility of the Hilbert space. The model reaches a test-set accuracy of 90.9% +/- 0.2% over five independent seeds on the full 10,000-image MNIST test set. Under an identical linear readout, the trained quantum feature map (88.1%) clearly outperforms a classical linear baseline on the same PCA inputs (83.2%) as well as an untrained (reservoir-style) version of the same dynamics (53.0%), demonstrating that the learned, input-dependent exchange pulses implement a genuinely non-linear and trainable feature map. The protocol is also robust to experimentally relevant imperfections: accuracy remains at 89.9% under 10% quasi-static pulse-area noise and at 89.8% when every observable is estimated from 10^3 measurement shots. These findings suggest that competitive QML can be executed on the simplest possible semiconductor spin-chain hardware, bypassing the need for leakage-prone encodings or complex micro-magnet integration.

item.title: Quantum non-local games: Quantum relations, projection lattices and rule operators
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Unifies projection-test games, Todorov–Turowska projection-lattice games, probabilistic quantum hypergraph games, and graphical rule operators under an operator-bimodule framework, showing winning transformation spaces equal rectangular quantum relations and projection lattices capture precisely the reflexive bimodules.

Grade 0.332 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “data encoding and the expressivity of quantum models” · Alexandros Chatzinikolaou

Figure

Commutative diagram mapping the formal relationships and value-preserving reductions between the various quantum game frameworks via operator spaces.

Asks

How do disparate formalisms for quantum non-local games mathematically relate to one another at the level of winning rules and game values?

But

Input and output von Neumann algebras are restricted to finite dimensions; referee algebra ℛ may be infinite-dimensional.

Tools

Operator bimodules · Quantum relations · Reflexive operator spaces · von Neumann algebras · Frobenius-algebraic rule operators

Abstract

Quantum non-local games with quantum inputs or outputs have been formulated in several different languages, including rank-one and quantum XOR games, support maps between projection lattices, probabilistic quantum hypergraphs, and Frobenius-algebraic rule operators on finite quantum sets. We give a unified operator-algebraic comparison of these models by assigning to each rule its winning transformation space: the operator space of transformations accepted with certainty. We introduce \( R\)-projection-test quantum games with finite-dimensional input and output von Neumann algebras and an arbitrary, possibly infinite-dimensional, referee von Neumann algebra \( R\). Their winning transformation spaces are precisely operator spaces with a natural bimodule structure, equivalently rectangular quantum relations. We compare this formalism with projection-lattice games, hypergraph quantum games, and the graphical rule-operator definition. Projection-lattice games capture exactly the reflexive winning bimodules. Hypergraph quantum games admit value-preserving projection-test realisations, and, after passing to perfect transformations, describe the same reflexive part as projection-lattice games. Using Daws' technique, we also translate rule operators to projections in tensor products of finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras. This identification places graphical rules in the same operator-bimodule framework and preserves both values and perfectness. Finally, we compare concurrency with the synchronicity conditions of Goldberg and of Bochniak--Kasprzak--Sołtan. The framework is illustrated by classical, rank-one, quantum XOR, colouring, and quantum graph homomorphism and isomorphism games.

item.title: Emergence of Strategic Equilibria from Transverse Field Ising Hamiltonian Dynamics
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Transverse-field Ising dynamics tune game equilibria via the interaction-time product Jt. At Jt=π/2 (local iSWAP gate), mutual cooperation (C,C) becomes the unique Nash equilibrium across Prisoner's Dilemma, Game of Chicken, and Stag Hunt.

Grade 0.332 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum machine learning” · Teena Thomas, S. Balakrishnan

Figure

Concurrence plotted against interaction-time product Jt. Entanglement scales monotonically from 0 at Jt=0 to 0.707 at Jt=π/4 and reaches unity at Jt=π/2.

Asks

How do quantum game equilibria emerge and evolve under continuous Hamiltonian-driven dynamics with tunable entanglement rather than fixed quantum gates?

Before

Gate-based Eisert–Wilkens–Lewenstein (EWL) protocol with fixed entangling operations.

But

Analyzed for two-player symmetric 2×2 games without environmental decoherence or dissipation.

Tools

transverse-field quantum Ising model · operator-based modified EWL scheme · Weyl chamber representation · two-qubit concurrence

Abstract

Game theory studies strategic decision-making among rational agents, and many classical games can be mapped onto interaction models such as the Ising model. Quantum game theory extends this framework by allowing players to exploit quantum superposition and entanglement. In this work, we study quantum games using an operator-based formulation derived from the transverse-field quantum Ising model. We show that the Hamiltonian-driven dynamics naturally generate entangling operator which resolve the dilemma in the game settings. This leads to a clear quantum advantage over classical outcomes. Unlike standard quantization schemes based on fixed entangling gates, the present approach enables tunable entanglement, controlled directly by physical Hamiltonian parameters, providing a hardware-relevant perspective on quantum game design.
